items.title: What RSA depends on
items.claim: RSA encryption (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977) relies on the practical difficulty of which mathematical operation?

options.text: Factoring the product of two large primes

items.reveal:
RSA's security rests on the gap between multiplying two large primes (easy) and recovering them from the product (currently hard for sufficient bit lengths).

Shor's 1994 algorithm shows a sufficiently large quantum computer would break RSA.
items.why: Modern cryptography is a bet that certain mathematical problems remain hard. Quantum computing threatens that bet.

items.title: P versus NP
items.claim: The P vs NP question is the most famous open problem in computer science. Which statement describes its current status?

options.text: It has been proven that P equals NP
It has been proven that P does not equal NP
It is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems and remains open

items.reveal_title: Open since 1971 and worth a million dollars
items.reveal:
Stephen Cook (1971) and Leonid Levin (1973) independently formalised the question. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers one of seven Millennium Prizes for its resolution.

Most researchers conjecture P does not equal NP, but no proof exists.
items.why: If P=NP, problems whose solutions can be checked quickly could also be found quickly — including breaking most modern encryption.

items.title: Latency differences
items.claim: L1 cache access takes about 1 ns. Roughly how long does a fetch from main memory take by comparison?
items.reveal:
Approximate figures (Jeff Dean's 'numbers everyone should know'): L1 cache 1 ns, main memory 100 ns, SSD 100 microseconds, disk seek 10 ms.

The ratios drive cache-friendly algorithm design.
items.why: Algorithm choice often matters less than memory layout once data exceeds cache size.
